## Everyday use

- **Shortcuts:** `Super+F1` opens a cheat sheet. `Super+D` launches apps,
  `Super+Enter` opens a terminal, `Super+Shift+E` opens the power menu (log
  out, suspend, reboot, power off). The Shortcuts page of Isotope Welcome
  shows them on the first login. In Sway, i3 and niri, `Super+Alt+L` locks the screen
  and `Print` takes a screenshot. Sway and i3 also lock the screen when idle
  and before suspend.
- **Apps:** Isotope includes no browser. At your first login, the Apps page
  of Isotope Welcome offers a browser (Firefox, Chromium, Brave or LibreWolf)
  and some essential apps, and installs them from Flathub for your user. Skip
  it if you like; "Install apps" in the Isotope menu or `isotope welcome apps`
  opens it again. Anything else:
  `flatpak install flathub <app>`; `distrobox` for a mutable Linux to tinker
  in.
- **Updates:** a tray icon shows the installed release and tells you when a
  new Isotope release is out; its menu checks, installs, reboots and
  pins. Everything the icon does is also in the terminal:

  ```sh
  isotope                        # installed vs latest release (same as `status`)
  isotope upgrade                # install the latest; asks, then offers a reboot
  isotope upgrade --version v0.1.2   # a specific release (also rolls back)
  isotope switch <flavor>        # move to another flavor's image line
  isotope switch --gpu vm        # move to the VM image (--gpu full: back)
  isotope reboot                 # reboot into the installed upgrade
  isotope rollback               # boot the previous system once (no download)
  ```

  Installing and rebooting go through a root service, `isotope-updated`, and
  polkit allows them for members of the `admin` group only; other users get a
  refusal, not a password prompt. The terminal and the tray use the same
  service, so a job started in one shows in the other.

  Upgrades are A/B: `kairos-agent upgrade` writes the new image next to the
  running one, which stays untouched until the reboot, and the previous system
  is kept as the fallback boot entry.

  Advanced mode is on by default: it lets you install any OCI image, not only
  an Isotope release (`isotope upgrade --image REF`, or "Install
  an image..." in the tray menu). To allow releases only, put `advanced=false`
  in `/etc/isotope/update.conf`. An image you install on purpose is
  pinned (`/var/lib/isotope-update/pin`): the tray shows it as pinned and stops
  offering "updates" over it until you pick the latest release again.
  Upgrade images are signed with cosign (keyless) and carry the labels
  `io.kairos.isotope.{flavor,version,hadron-version,gpu,firmware}`, which the
  updater uses to recognise an Isotope image. The agent flavor has no
  tray and no service; its CLI keeps the direct `sudo` path.
- **Backups:** `isotope backup` and `isotope restore`, through sudo for the
  `admin` group, with restic (built in the Dockerfile's `restic` stage). A
  backup is everything that survives a reboot: the persistent partition
  (`/usr/local`, where `/home` is `.state/home.bind` and every other
  persistent path a `.state/<path>.bind`) and `/oem`, without caches, logs and,
  unless `--with-containers`, Docker's and Podman's storage.
  `/usr/local/isotope-backup/` holds the target, the schedule and the result
  (`config`), the repository password (`password`, 0600) and the credentials
  of a remote target (`env`); not `/var/lib`, which Kairos rebuilds at every
  boot. `isotope backup --export FILE` writes one file: a tar of a restic
  repository made for it. `isotope-backup.timer` runs
  `isotope backup --scheduled` every day; it does nothing until
  `isotope backup schedule daily|weekly`, and skips a directory target that
  holds no repository (an unplugged disk). The agent image has none of it.
  See `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-16-isotope-cli-backup-design.md`.

## Boot splash

`splash/` builds the boot animation and installs it as `/usr/bin/kairos-splash`.
kairos-init keeps a binary already at that path, and its dracut module and
`kairos-splash.service` then run it in the initramfs and in the booted system.
So there is one animation from firmware to login, with no splash units of our
own. It draws straight into the framebuffer (simpledrm, then whichever DRM
driver takes over) over the same gradient as the GRUB theme, and falls back to
a text animation on a console without one. Add `kairos.splash=0` at the boot
menu to turn it off for one boot. See [`splash/README.md`](../splash/README.md).

The boot menu also sets the Linux console's 16 colours to the Isotope palette
(`vt.default_red/grn/blu` on the kernel command line, generated from
`theme/palette.toml`), so the boot messages, the ly login and the installer
sit on the desktop's violet ink rather than black.

## Following Hadron

The Hadron release is pinned in one value kept in four places (the
`Makefile`, `Dockerfile`, `Dockerfile.agent` and the agent gate's
`test/agent/Dockerfile.compat`). `scripts/bump-hadron.sh vX.Y.Z` moves them all; `--check` fails if they ever disagree, and CI runs it.

`.github/workflows/follow-hadron.yml` runs daily. When kairos-io/hadron
publishes a newer release (and its images are pullable), it pins it, commits to
`main`, tags the next patch version and dispatches the release pipeline below.
A failed release publishes nothing, so installed systems never see it.

## Updating components

Every other source version is an `ARG <NAME>_VERSION=` in the Dockerfiles,
under a `# renovate:` comment that names where its releases are tagged.
Renovate (`renovate.json`) opens update pull requests on Monday mornings;
major updates wait for approval on its Dependency Dashboard issue. A new pin
needs the comment, or an entry in `scripts/check-renovate-pins.sh` with the
reason it is updated by hand. CI runs that script.

## Releases

Pushing a `v`-prefixed tag runs `.github/workflows/release.yml`. The workflow
builds the Sway, i3/XLibre, COSMIC and niri installer ISOs in parallel and
builds the agent ISO in a job that first runs all five agent gates. It then verifies every
asset and creates a GitHub Release:

```sh
git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "Isotope v1.0.0"
git push origin v1.0.0
```

Every desktop flavor is released in two lines:

| Line | Build | ISO and upgrade image | For |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| full | `GPU=full FIRMWARE=true` | `isotope-<flavor>-<tag>-amd64.iso`, `:<flavor>-<tag>` | desktops and laptops: Intel and AMD GPU drivers, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, GPU and audio firmware, CPU microcode. Also runs in a VM (llvmpipe, virgl) |
| vm | `GPU=vm` | `isotope-<flavor>-vm-<tag>-amd64.iso`, `:<flavor>-vm-<tag>` | virtual machines: about 0.3 GB smaller, no hardware GPU drivers, no firmware |

The agent is a VM appliance and has one line, built with `GPU=vm`:
`isotope-agent-<tag>-amd64.iso` and `:agent-<tag>`.

The server edition has one line too: `isotope-server-<tag>-amd64.iso`
and `:server-<tag>`. It is built with `GPU=full FIRMWARE=true` (the Makefile
sets both for `DESKTOP=server`), which names the line; it has no Mesa, and its
firmware is the network card set. A server upgrades only to server images,
and a desktop never installs one: `isotope-update` refuses both, and `switch`
refuses on a server.

Every release also pushes the upgrade images above to
`ghcr.io/kairos-community/isotope` (the agent image only after all five
gates pass). `isotope-update` installs those; it only considers tags GitHub
reports as the latest *published* release. An installed system stays on its
line: `/etc/isotope/release` records `GPU=full` or `GPU=vm`, and upgrades
pull the image of that line. Systems installed from v0.0.7 or earlier have no
`GPU` key and follow the full line (their own updater already pulls
`<flavor>-<tag>`). `isotope-update switch --gpu vm|full` or the tray menu moves a
system to the other line. Each pushed image is signed with cosign (keyless, by
digest) and labelled with its flavor, line and release tag;
`scripts/release-manifest.sh` fails the release if they disagree.

Each release carries forty files — ten ISOs (four flavors in two lines, the
server edition and the agent), and for every ISO a checksum, an SPDX SBOM, and a build
manifest:

| Asset | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `isotope-<flavor>[-vm]-<tag>-amd64.iso` | the bootable installer |
| `….iso.sha256` | its SHA-256, in `sha256sum --check` format |
| `….iso.spdx.json` | SPDX JSON SBOM of the OCI image the ISO wraps, produced by `anchore/syft:v1.29.0` |
| `….iso.build.json` | the build manifest described below |

`<flavor>` is `sway`, `i3`, `cosmic`, `niri`, `server`, or `agent`. The build manifest records exactly what
went into the image, so a downloaded ISO can be traced back to its sources:

```json
{
  "release_tag": "v1.0.0",
  "git_commit": "…",
  "hadron_base_reference": "ghcr.io/kairos-io/hadron:v0.6.3",
  "hadron_base_digest": "sha256:…",
  "image_id": "sha256:…",
  "iso": "isotope-agent-v1.0.0-amd64.iso",
  "iso_sha256": "…",
  "desktop_flavor": "agent",
  "gpu": "vm",
  "firmware": false,
  "xlibre_version": "25.2.0",
  "cua_revision": "…",
  "atspi_version": "2.54.0"
}
```

All thirteen keys are present in every manifest. `gpu` is the line (`full` or
`vm`, always `vm` for agent and `full` for server), and `firmware` is `true` exactly on the full line.
`xlibre_version` is set only for i3
and agent, the two flavors that run the XLibre X server, and
`cua_revision`/`atspi_version` are `null` for every flavor except agent.

The publishing job refuses to upload unless it finds exactly ten ISOs, ten
checksums, ten SBOMs, and ten manifests, one for each flavor and line, every
checksum verifies, every SBOM
parses as SPDX with a non-empty package list, and every manifest carries valid
values that match the ISO shipped beside it. The agent job uploads nothing at
all — not even its ISO — until the compatibility, contract, install, recovery,
and UI gates have all passed. Release artifacts are not signed.

An existing tag can be rebuilt from the Actions page with the workflow's manual
dispatch. Rebuilt assets replace same-named assets on a mutable release.

## Try it in a VM

```sh
make vm-install   # fresh disk, boot the newest installer ISO (then it reboots to disk)
make vm           # boot the already-installed disk

DESKTOP=i3 make vm-install
DESKTOP=i3 make vm
```

Connect over VNC (`<host>:5910`); set `NOVNC=1` for a browser client. See the
header of `tools/vm.sh` for knobs (`MEM`, `VNC`, `FRESH=1`, `ISO=…`, …).

The Kairos init layer is folded into the Dockerfile's final stage, so either
Docker command above already produces a bootable artifact
AuroraBoot can turn into an ISO (build `--target default` for the bare desktop
image without it).

## Run on real hardware

The image is a bootable Kairos/Hadron OS image. Build an ISO/disk with AuroraBoot
(`make iso`) and install it to a machine. On boot, `ly` runs on `tty1` and starts
the session selected at image build time. (Real wifi/bluetooth/audio require the
`linux-firmware` blobs — see milestone M6.)

## Test (Sway headless harness)

The existing `test/` harness exercises the default Sway variant, builds a bootable ISO
with AuroraBoot, boots it headless in QEMU, and asserts that the desktop and each
subsystem come up — entirely without a display. It exercises even wifi and
bluetooth using virtual kernel devices (`mac80211_hwsim`, `hci_vhci`).

```sh
# Run all assertions up to a given milestone (default M0)
MILESTONE=M1 test/run.sh

# Faster iteration
SKIP_BUILD=1 test/run.sh   # reuse built images
SKIP_ISO=1   test/run.sh   # reuse existing ISO
```

The guest emits `SWAYTEST: PASS/FAIL <name>` markers on the serial console; the
harness parses them and exits non-zero on any failure. Screenshots captured with
`grim` are written to a scratch disk and extracted to `test/artifacts/`.

The `test/agent/` directory holds the agent overlay's own test suite
(`run.sh compatibility` boots the real graphical XLibre/i3 session in QEMU and
drives it with `cua-driver`; `run.sh compatibility agent-desktop:dev` reuses an
image from `make agent-image` and builds only the test layer; focused scripts like `systemd_units_test.sh` and
`session_launcher_test.sh` check narrower slices statically). Notably,
`profile_isolation.sh` builds (or, with `SKIP_BUILD=1`, reuses) all three
images — `sway-desktop:dev`, `i3-desktop:dev`, `agent-desktop:dev` — exports
each one's real filesystem with `docker export`, and asserts against that
export: the plain Sway/i3 images contain none of the agent-only files,
units, or accounts, the agent image contains all of them, and the generic
agent image's file contents carry no live bearer, no configured digest, and
no PEM private key:

```sh
bash test/agent/profile_isolation.sh
SKIP_BUILD=1 bash test/agent/profile_isolation.sh   # reuse already-built images
```

### Users and login

The image bakes in **no user**. The desktop user is created at install time and
lives on the persistent `/home`. Kairos' default `kairos` user (password
`kairos`) exists only on the live ISO and in UKI install mode: the Dockerfile
`kairos` stage limits kairos-init's `10_accounting.yaml` to those boots, so an
installed system, and its login screen, shows only the users you created. An
upgraded system loses the old locked `kairos` user on its first boot, because
`/etc` is rebuilt at every boot; `/home/kairos`, if it exists, stays. On boot the **`ly`** display manager (TUI, on
tty1) authenticates that user and launches the selected session through
`/usr/bin/start-desktop`. In the Sway image this is the Wayland session; in the
i3 image, `ly` starts XLibre and then launches i3.

There are two ways to create that user:

- **Interactive installer (default).** Boot the live ISO with nothing else and
  `isotope-install-ui` — a Go TUI at `/usr/bin/isotope-install-ui`, wired in via
  `system/oem/90_desktop_installer.yaml` — runs on tty1. It collects **hostname,
  username, password, optional GitHub SSH keys and target disk** behind a review
  gate, assigns the desktop groups (admin, audio, video, render, input,
  bluetooth, seat), hashes the password (`openssl passwd -6`), writes the
  cloud-config, then runs `kairos-agent install` behind a branded progress
  screen (`l` toggles the raw logs, `s` opens a rescue shell if the install
  fails). Source lives in `install-ui/`.

  On the desktop ISOs (sway, i3, cosmic, niri) `isotope-install-ui` first
  starts the **graphical installer**: `cage -s -- /usr/bin/isotope-install-gui`,
  a Gio window over `install-ui/core`, so it asks the same questions with the
  same checks and runs the same install. It falls back to the text installer
  when cage exits before the window's first frame (no DRM device, no seat), when
  the image has no cage (the server, the agent) or when the kernel command line
  has `isotope.installer=text` (the live menu's "isotope (text installer)"
  entry). A new keyboard layout restarts cage with it (exit status 75 and
  `/run/isotope-install/state.json`), because Gio does not let a program
  translate keys itself. "Open a terminal" on the failure page starts foot in
  cage where the image has it (sway, niri), and otherwise exits with status 76
  for the text installer's rescue shell on tty1. Source lives in
  `install-gui/`; see
  `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-17-graphical-installer-design.md`.

  The GUI's tests need cgo and Mesa (llvmpipe, EGL's surfaceless platform).

- **Unattended cloud-config.** Provide a `cloud-config.yaml` (`users:`/`install:`
  block — see the example file) via AuroraBoot `--cloud-config` or a datasource.
  When one is present the TUI detects it and runs the normal unattended
  install instead of prompting — so CI and automated installs are unaffected.

The top-level build targets are:

```sh
make DESKTOP=sway iso
make DESKTOP=i3 iso
make agent-iso VERSION=v1.2.3
```

`agent-iso` first builds the i3 base image, then layers `Dockerfile.agent` on
top to produce the opt-in agent appliance. The agent ISO still uses the same
unattended install mechanism: if the datasource already contains `users:` and
`install:` the wizard skips the prompt path. For the agent appliance, the seed
also needs `isotope_agent.enabled=true` so the overlay starts its agent profile
instead of the plain desktop path.

Minimal unattended agent seed:

```yaml
#cloud-config
install:
  auto: true
  device: /dev/vda
  reboot: true
users:
  - name: agent
    passwd: "$6$..."
isotope_agent:
  enabled: true
  auth:
    user_token_hash: "sha256:..."
```

**Tokens and keys are runtime seed data, never Docker build args.** The bearer
digests (`user_token_hash`/`admin_token_hash`) and any TLS material for the
gateway are written into the datasource/cloud-config that AuroraBoot or the
installer feeds the *booted* image; they are read by the OEM provisioning
stage at boot (`system/oem/90_agent_profile.yaml`), not baked into a layer by
`agent-image`/`agent-iso`. Those two targets only ever take `BASE_IMAGE`,
`AGENT_BASE_IMAGE` and `VERSION` as `--build-arg`s (see the `Makefile`) — no
credential ever needs to (or should) flow through `docker build`. This is
also why the generic `agent-desktop`/agent ISO ships with no bearer, no
configured digest and no private key embedded in it:
`test/agent/profile_isolation.sh` exports the actual built images and proves
it (both that the plain Sway/i3 images carry none of the agent files, and
that the generic agent image's filesystem contents contain no live secret).

`ly`'s interactive TUI login can't be driven over a headless VT, and headless
QEMU has no active VT / `virtio-gpu` gets zero scanouts (`-display none`). So the

wlroots **headless backend + pixman** renderer — the canonical way Sway is
exercised in CI. The harness still asserts `ly` is installed and wired up. The
real `ly` → DRM login path is validated on physical hardware.

### Real hardware

The default image is VM-slim. For real laptops, build with the firmware subset:

```sh
docker build --build-arg FIRMWARE=true -t sway-desktop:hw .
docker build --build-arg DESKTOP=i3 --build-arg FIRMWARE=true -t i3-desktop:hw .
```

This bundles a chosen part of a pinned `linux-firmware` release, what common
laptops and desktops need to show a display and to have Wi-Fi, Bluetooth,
Ethernet and sound: AMD, Intel and nouveau GSP (Turing and later) graphics;
Intel, Qualcomm laptop, Realtek, MediaTek laptop and USB, Broadcom (brcmfmac and
brcmsmac) and Marvell PCIe Wi-Fi and Bluetooth; Realtek Ethernet; Cirrus and TI
speaker amplifiers.
It adds Intel's SOF audio DSP firmware from a pinned `sof-bin` release, and
the AMD and Intel CPU microcode, which dracut puts in the early cpio of the
initramfs (the kernel loads microcode only there). The Dockerfile `firmware`
stage lists the parts and what it leaves out. The blobs go to
`/usr/lib/firmware`, compressed with zstd: about 290 MB, against about 960 MB
for all of `linux-firmware`. They must not go to `/usr/local/lib/firmware`,
which an installed system mounts its persistent partition over.

`tools/install-firmware.sh` also makes the links `linux-firmware` declares to
the installed files: drivers often ask for the link (iwlwifi asks for
`iwlwifi-<card>.ucode` at the top of the directory). The build fails when a
firmware name that the base image's kernel modules declare, and that the
chosen parts provide, is not installed. `test/firmware/check-install-firmware.sh`
checks the scripts on a fake tree. Firmware loading on real Wi-Fi, Bluetooth,
GPU and audio hardware is checked by booting on a physical machine; CI does
not test it.

### Hardware GPU (accelerated GL)

The default Mesa build (`GPU=vm`) ships only software and virtual drivers:
`llvmpipe`, `virgl`, `softpipe` and `svga`. In a VM with 3D acceleration
(virtio-gpu with OpenGL) Mesa uses `virgl` and renders on the host GPU. On any
other display (virtio-gpu or QXL without 3D, `-vga std`, or real hardware with
`GPU=vm`) it uses `llvmpipe`, a multi-threaded rasterizer that compiles shaders
with LLVM. `softpipe` is only a fallback that `GALLIUM_DRIVER=softpipe`
selects: it is 60-190 times slower than `llvmpipe` (a key press in the COSMIC
greeter took about 6 s to reach the screen). For accelerated GL on real
Intel, AMD and NVIDIA laptops, build with `GPU=full`, as the release builds the
full line:

```sh
docker build --build-arg GPU=full --build-arg FIRMWARE=true \
  -t sway-desktop:hw .

docker build --build-arg DESKTOP=i3 --build-arg GPU=full \
  --build-arg FIRMWARE=true -t i3-desktop:hw .
```

`GPU=full` also builds Mesa `iris` (Intel), `radeonsi` (AMD) and `nouveau`
(NVIDIA, the open kernel driver; no NVK Vulkan). Every mode links LLVM
(`llvmpipe` needs it); `iris` and `radeonsi` also need libclc and SPIRV;
`nouveau` needs only `libdrm_nouveau`, which the libdrm stage builds. Without
`nouveau`, a compositor on an NVIDIA GPU finds no GL or GBM driver for the
render node: the screen shows the hardware cursor and nothing else.
The example builds its **own** LLVM/clang/libclc + SPIRV stack on top of the
published `hadron-toolchain` (same musl ABI — no Alpine cross-mix) as dedicated
stages in this Dockerfile, so **the main Hadron toolchain is never touched and
no extra orchestration is needed** — a plain `docker build` is enough. The
SPIRV stages are gated: for `GPU=vm` (the default) BuildKit prunes them. LLVM
itself compiles for about three hours; CI and release builds take it from a
prebuilt image instead (`LLVM_IMAGE`, see the Makefile).

Mesa is built with `-Dllvm=enabled` and `-Dcpp_rtti=false` (the libLLVM is built
without RTTI). The image bundles only `libLLVM.so` (~125 MB), and for
`GPU=full` also `libelf.so`, because the megadriver links them at runtime.

Validated: Mesa 25.3 builds `iris`/`radeonsi`/`virgl`/`softpipe` into
`libgallium-25.3.0.so` against the example-built libLLVM, the megadriver resolves
all runtime symbols, and the resulting ISO boots. Actual GPU *rendering* is
validated on physical hardware — QEMU has no real GPU, so a VM boot uses
llvmpipe or virgl while the hardware drivers ride along for real metal.

# Trusted Boot release keys

The Trusted Boot edition (`isotope-<flavor>-uki-<tag>-amd64.iso` and the
`<flavor>-uki-<tag>` upgrade images) is signed with keys this project
generates and holds. A machine installed from it boots only images signed with
these keys, and its disk key is sealed to them. Losing them means no more
upgrades for those machines; leaking them means anyone can sign an image those
machines will boot. Treat them that way.

The design is in
[superpowers/specs/2026-11-07-trusted-boot-edition-design.md](superpowers/specs/2026-11-07-trusted-boot-edition-design.md).

## The keys

| File | Where it lives | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `db.key`, `db.pem` | GitHub secrets `UKI_DB_KEY`, `UKI_DB_PEM`, and offline | signs every UKI (the Secure Boot db key) |
| `tpm2-pcr-private.pem` | secret `UKI_TPM_PCR_KEY`, and offline | signs the PCR policy the disk key is sealed to |
| `PK.auth`, `KEK.auth`, `db.auth` | secrets `UKI_PK_AUTH`, `UKI_KEK_AUTH`, `UKI_DB_AUTH` (base64), and offline | public: what systemd-boot enrolls into the firmware |
| `PK.key`, `KEK.key` | offline only | sign later changes to the enrolled keys (a new db, a revocation) |

`db.auth` and `KEK.auth` include Microsoft's certificates, so graphics cards and
other option ROMs signed by Microsoft keep working after enrollment.

## Creating them, once

On a trusted machine with Docker, `gh` logged in with admin rights on the
repository, and `openssl`:

```sh
scripts/uki-release-keys.sh generate ~/isotope-uki-keys
scripts/uki-release-keys.sh upload ~/isotope-uki-keys
gh variable set TRUSTED_BOOT_RELEASE --body true --repo kairos-community/isotope
```

Then copy `~/isotope-uki-keys` to two offline places (an encrypted USB stick
and a password manager vault, say) and delete it from the machine. The
certificates are valid for ten years (`DAYS` changes that); UEFI firmware does
not check their dates, but the release job warns 60 days before the db
certificate expires.

`DRY_RUN=1 scripts/uki-release-keys.sh upload DIR` shows what would be set
without setting anything.

## What CI does with them

The `build-uki` job in `.github/workflows/release.yml` runs only when
`TRUSTED_BOOT_RELEASE` is `true`. It writes the six secrets to `/dev/shm`
(umask 077, never the workspace), checks that `db.pem` belongs to `db.key`,
and signs the UKI ISO and upgrade image of every full line (sway, i3, cosmic,
niri) and the server. The release job then requires those five ISOs and
images; a missing one stops the release.

## Things this does not cover yet

- **Rotating the db key.** It needs a `db` update signed with `KEK.key`,
  installed on every machine, and a release signed with both keys while
  machines move over. Not automated.
- **A leaked db key.** Revoking it needs a `dbx` update signed with `KEK.key`.
  Until that exists, a leak cannot be undone on installed machines.
- **Your own keys.** A user who wants their own root of trust builds with
  `make uki-keys uki-iso` and must build every upgrade with the same keys:
  the project's `<flavor>-uki-<tag>` images do not boot on their machines.

# Isotope system extensions

Each directory here is one system extension: software that runs on the host
but is not in the image, merged over `/usr` when a user installs it with
`isotope ext` (or the Extensions entry of the Isotope menu). Isotope builds
them on the same Hadron release as the image and publishes them in its own
catalog, which `/etc/isotope/extensions.conf` names before hadron-layers. So
a name published here wins over the same name in hadron-layers.

## What a directory holds

```
extensions/<name>/
  Dockerfile       stages `default` (the files) and `test` (offline checks)
  extension.json   {"title": "...", "description": "..."} for the menu
```

- `<name>` is what users install: `isotope ext install <name>`.
- `ARG HADRON_VERSION` has no default. The workflow passes the image's pin
  (`scripts/bump-hadron.sh --current`). Build on
  `ghcr.io/kairos-io/hadron-toolchain:${HADRON_VERSION}`.
- `ARG <NAME>_VERSION=<version>` is the extension's version (`htop` reads
  `HTOP_VERSION`, `foo-bar` reads `FOO_BAR_VERSION`). It must start with a
  digit, and it needs a `# renovate:` comment above it
  (`scripts/check-renovate-pins.sh`).
- The `default` stage is `FROM scratch` with only files under `/usr`. A
  system extension merges nothing else.
- The `test` stage runs on `ghcr.io/kairos-io/hadron:${HADRON_VERSION}`. It
  must fail when a file of the extension already exists in the base. A file
  over the base's copy is what `isotope ext` refuses, and in the worst case it
  replaces a library the desktop uses. Link the extension's own libraries
  statically, as `htop/` does with ncurses.

Build and test one locally:

```
docker build --build-arg HADRON_VERSION=$(scripts/bump-hadron.sh --current) --target test extensions/htop
```

## How it is published

`.github/workflows/extensions.yml`, on every change here that reaches `main`:

1. builds the `test` stage, then `default`;
2. makes `<name>.sysext.raw` with AuroraBoot (`auroraboot sysext`);
3. pushes it to `ghcr.io/kairos-community/isotope:sysext-<name>-<version>-amd64`
   (the image's own public repository, so nothing new has to be made public);
4. writes the catalog with `scripts/extensions-catalog.sh`, which lists every
   `sysext-*` tag of the repository pinned by digest, and deploys it to
   <https://kairos-community.github.io/isotope/extensions.json>.

A pull request runs steps 1 and 2 only.

The extensions are unsigned, like hadron-layers'. They merge because the image
sets `extensions.ignore_signatures`, which a Trusted Boot image does not set.
So a Trusted Boot system cannot use them.

The shared look of Isotope's graphical tools: today the graphical installer
(`install-gui/`), and the tools that must look like it, such as a first-login
setup window. It is a Go module of its own, on Gio. It does not open a

- The embedded fonts (Urbanist, Inter, JetBrains Mono, with their
  licences in `fonts/`) and the shared text styles.
- Widgets that know nothing about an app: buttons, text fields, labelled

  scrolled page, a pick list, the Isotope mark and the small icons.

#!/bin/sh
# Hardware keys for the sway and i3 variants: volume, mute, screen brightness
# and media playback, with the new level shown as a notification with a
# progress bar (mako on sway, dunst on i3). niri (Noctalia) and COSMIC handle
# these keys in their own shell; COSMIC calls this script only for the
# playback keys, which it would otherwise send to playerctl.
#
#   isotope-media-key volume-up | volume-down | mute | mic-mute
#   isotope-media-key brightness-up | brightness-down
#   isotope-media-key play-pause | next | previous | stop
#
# No extra tools: volume through wpctl, brightness through logind's
# SetBrightness (allowed for the user of the active session, no polkit or
# udev rule needed), players through MPRIS on the session bus, and the
# on-screen level through the notification server, all with busctl.
set -u

STEP=5  # percent per key press

# osd SUMMARY BODY PERCENT: show or update the one on-screen level
# notification. Its id is kept in the runtime directory and passed as
# replaces_id, so a held key updates one pop-up instead of stacking new ones.
# The stack tags do the same for dunst and for servers that know them.
osd() {
    idfile="${XDG_RUNTIME_DIR:-/tmp}/isotope-osd-id"
    id=0
    [ -r "$idfile" ] && id=$(cat "$idfile" 2>/dev/null)
    case "$id" in ''|*[!0-9]*) id=0 ;; esac
    out=$(busctl --user call org.freedesktop.Notifications /org/freedesktop/Notifications \
        org.freedesktop.Notifications Notify 'susssasa{sv}i' \
        "Isotope" "$id" "" "$1" "$2" 0 \
        3 value i "$3" x-dunst-stack-tag s isotope-osd x-canonical-private-synchronous s isotope-osd \
        1500 2>/dev/null) || return 0
    printf '%s\n' "${out#u }" > "$idfile" 2>/dev/null || true
}

# volume_osd TARGET NAME: show the volume of a wpctl target.
# `wpctl get-volume` prints "Volume: 0.40", plus " [MUTED]" when muted.
volume_osd() {
    v=$(wpctl get-volume "$1" 2>/dev/null) || return 0
    pct=$(printf '%s\n' "$v" | awk '{ printf "%d", $2 * 100 + 0.5 }')
    case "$v" in
        *MUTED*) osd "$2" "Muted" 0 ;;
        *)       osd "$2" "$pct%" "$pct" ;;
    esac
}

# backlight: print the backlight device the kernel and systemd prefer
# (firmware, then platform, then raw), or nothing on a machine without one.
backlight() {
    for want in firmware platform raw; do
        for d in /sys/class/backlight/*; do
            [ -r "$d/type" ] || continue
            [ "$(cat "$d/type")" = "$want" ] && { basename "$d"; return; }
        done
    done
}

brightness() {
    dev=$(backlight)
    [ -n "$dev" ] || exit 0
    max=$(cat "/sys/class/backlight/$dev/max_brightness")
    cur=$(cat "/sys/class/backlight/$dev/brightness")
    [ "$max" -gt 0 ] || exit 0
    step=$((max * STEP / 100)); [ "$step" -ge 1 ] || step=1
    # Never go fully dark: on many panels 0 turns the backlight off.
    floor=$((max / 100)); [ "$floor" -ge 1 ] || floor=1
    case "$1" in
        up)   new=$((cur + step)) ;;
        down) new=$((cur - step)) ;;
    esac
    [ "$new" -le "$max" ] || new=$max
    [ "$new" -ge "$floor" ] || new=$floor
    for s in auto self; do
        busctl call org.freedesktop.login1 "/org/freedesktop/login1/session/$s" \
            org.freedesktop.login1.Session SetBrightness ssu backlight "$dev" "$new" \
            >/dev/null 2>&1 && break
    done
    pct=$(((new * 100 + max / 2) / max))
    osd "Brightness" "$pct%" "$pct"
}

# player: print the MPRIS player to control: the first one that is playing,
# else the first one on the bus.
player() {
    first=""
    for p in $(busctl --user list --no-legend 2>/dev/null |
            awk '$1 ~ /^org\.mpris\.MediaPlayer2\./ { print $1 }'); do
        [ -n "$first" ] || first=$p
        status=$(busctl --user get-property "$p" /org/mpris/MediaPlayer2 \
            org.mpris.MediaPlayer2.Player PlaybackStatus 2>/dev/null)
        [ "$status" = 's "Playing"' ] && { echo "$p"; return; }
    done
    echo "$first"
}

media() {
    p=$(player)
    [ -n "$p" ] || exit 0
    busctl --user call "$p" /org/mpris/MediaPlayer2 org.mpris.MediaPlayer2.Player "$1" \
        >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
}

case "${1:-}" in
    volume-up)
        # 150%, the same ceiling as scrolling on the waybar volume module.
        wpctl set-volume -l 1.5 @DEFAULT_AUDIO_SINK@ "$STEP%+"
        volume_osd @DEFAULT_AUDIO_SINK@ Volume ;;
    volume-down)
        wpctl set-volume @DEFAULT_AUDIO_SINK@ "$STEP%-"
        volume_osd @DEFAULT_AUDIO_SINK@ Volume ;;
    mute)
        wpctl set-mute @DEFAULT_AUDIO_SINK@ toggle
        volume_osd @DEFAULT_AUDIO_SINK@ Volume ;;
    mic-mute)
        wpctl set-mute @DEFAULT_AUDIO_SOURCE@ toggle
        volume_osd @DEFAULT_AUDIO_SOURCE@ Microphone ;;
    brightness-up)   brightness up ;;
    brightness-down) brightness down ;;
    play-pause) media PlayPause ;;
    next)       media Next ;;
    previous)   media Previous ;;
    stop)       media Stop ;;
    *)
        echo "usage: isotope-media-key volume-up|volume-down|mute|mic-mute|brightness-up|brightness-down|play-pause|next|previous|stop" >&2
        exit 2 ;;
esac
